result.summary: Pausanias lists Athenian islands, especially Salamis, with its history, its cult of Ajax and Eurysaces and a legendary flower. He then digresses to the huge bones and bodies of the dead, including Ajax's knees, Protophanes, Asterius and the bones at the Gates of Temenus.

scenes.title: Islands of the Athenians
scenes.summary: Pausanias names Athenian islands, including Helena, where Helen landed after Ilium's fall, and places Salamis opposite Eleusis.

scenes.title: Salamis and Ajax
scenes.summary: The history of Salamis is traced from Telamon to Athenian rule, the expulsion of its people, and the honours for Ajax and Eurysaces. A stone of Telamon and a flower are shown.
scenes.stakes: The Salaminians are condemned for treason and expelled; Ascetades is put to death.

scenes.title: Giant Bones and Odd Corpses
scenes.summary: Pausanias reports the tomb of Ajax, his enormous kneecaps, and the strange corpse of Protophanes.

scenes.title: Asterius and the bones of Hyllus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Asterius's tomb on Lade and the huge bones in Lydia, which locals took for Geryon and later for Hyllus.

notable_quotes.reason: Local legend of a hyacinth-like flower marked with letters springing up after Ajax's death.

analysis.text: Pausanias blends local history with marvels, using giant bones and relics to link the present to heroic times.
The punishment of Salamis shows Athens' harsh politics under Macedonian pressure after Cassander's wars; hero cults like Ajax's anchored civic identity.

fun_facts.text: Ancient people often took fossil bones for those of heroes; Pausanias himself corrects a local Lydian identification of Geryon.

language_notes.text: "Leaving Attica on the left" means sailing with the Attic coast on the port side, past Cape Sunium.
The hyacinth flower was said to bear the letters AI (alas), marking the grief of Apollo for Hyacinthus; here the Ajax flower is said to show similar markings.
The dispute over the arms of Achilles: Ajax and Ulysses (Odysseus) contended for them, and Ajax killed himself after losing.
"Pentathlum" is the pentathlon, the five-event contest; quoits are discuses. "Mills" translates a Greek medical term for the kneecap.
The pancratium was a brutal contest combining wrestling and boxing.
A cubit is roughly eighteen inches, so the corpse is about three feet long, which is small, not huge.
Geryon was a three-bodied monster whose cattle Hercules carried off as one of his labours.
Oceanus was the great river encircling the world in Greek belief, near where Geryon was thought to live.

context_notes.text: Telamon, father of Ajax, was a king from Ægina who settled Salamis. Salamis was the name of an Asopus-related figure and the island.
Cassander was the Macedonian ruler who held Athens' region in the late fourth century BC; Salamis fell to his forces.
Aulis was the Boeotian port where the Greek fleet gathered before sailing to Troy.
Pausanias argues that giant bodies are not explained by climate, since cold Celtic peoples are not larger than Egyptians.
Hercules served the Lydian queen Omphale, and Hyllus was his son, later a leader of the Heracleidae.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias reports Athenian judgment and the oath in an even, documentary tone, treating political history as part of the monument record.
The unexplained huge bones prepare for the competing local theories that follow.
The antiquarians claim to tell "the real truth" right after merely swapping one unproven identification for another.
